H1.text: A tightrope walker carries a long pole. A truck piled high with hay tips over on a turn. A toy bird balances on its beak.

H2.text: Three different scenes. All three hide one special point.

H3.text: Aarav cuts a funny shape out of cardboard for his science model. He wants to balance it on a pencil tip.

H4.text: He tries here, and there. It keeps falling. So where is the balance point?

H5.text: A plumb line finds it in two tries.

P1.text: Every tiny bit of the cardboard has weight. Gravity pulls each bit down.

P2.text: Bits on the left try to turn the card one way. Bits on the right, the other way.

P3.text: There is one point where all these turning effects cancel out. That point is the centre of gravity, G.

P4.text: Put the pencil right under G, and the card balances.

S1.text: Now hang the cut-out on a pin, through a hole called A, and hold it tilted.

S2.text: Its weight acts at G, straight down. G is off to one side of the pin, so the weight turns the card.

S3.text: It swings past the bottom, and back. Each swing is smaller.

S5.text: The lever arm is the sideways distance from the pin to the line of the weight. Turning effect equals weight times lever arm.

S6.text: As G swings under the pin, the lever arm shrinks to zero. So the card comes to rest there.

S7.text: On the graph, the turning effect swings plus and minus, then dies away to zero.

S8.text: Now hang a plumb line from the same pin, and draw along it. G must be somewhere on this line.

S9.text: Next, hang the card from a second hole, B, and let it settle.

S10.text: Draw the new line. The two lines cross at exactly one point. That point is G.

D1.text: Is G the same point as the centre of mass? Let's check, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. A bit of mass m sits a sideways distance x away. Its weight, m g, turns the body by m g times x.

D3.text: Step two. Add up every bit. The total turning effect is the sum of m g x.

D4.text: Step three. If g is the same for every bit, take it outside. The total becomes g times the sum of m x.

D5.text: Step four. Measured from the centre of mass, the sum of m x is zero. So the turning effect is zero there too.

D6.text: So when g is the same everywhere, the two points are the same.

T1.text: Remember this. The centre of gravity is the point where the total turning effect of gravity is zero.

R1.text: Now the plumb line trick, link by link.

R2.text: The card hangs still, so nothing is turning it.

R3.text: The pin pushes at the pin itself, so its push has no lever arm.

R4.text: The weight has no turning effect only when G is straight below the pin.

R5.text: So the vertical line through the pin must pass through G. Two such lines meet at G.

K1.text: Side by side. In a cardboard cut-out, g is the same at every bit. So G sits at the centre of mass.

K2.text: In a very tall tower, g gets a tiny bit weaker higher up. So each kilogram at the top weighs a little less.

K3.text: Now you try. In a very tall tower, is the centre of gravity slightly above or slightly below the centre of mass? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Slightly below! The lower parts are pulled a bit harder. In everyday objects, the gap is far too small to notice.

B1.text: G also decides when things tip over.

B2.text: Tilt a box. While the line straight down from G stays inside its base, the weight turns it back.

B3.text: Once that line passes the corner, the weight turns it over. It tips.

B4.text: Your turn. A bus with luggage on its roof, or the same luggage packed low. Which tips at a smaller tilt? Pause and decide.

B5.text: The roof luggage! It raises G, so the line from G passes the wheels sooner.

W2.text: A box is forty centimetres wide, with its centre of gravity in the middle, sixty centimetres up. At what tilt does it tip?

W3.text: It tips when the line from G reaches the corner.

W4.text: Then tan theta equals half the width over the height. Twenty over sixty. That is one third.

W5.text: So theta is about eighteen point four degrees.

X2.text: Many students think G must lie inside the material of the body.

X3.text: Not always. For a boomerang, or a bent wire, G lies in the empty space, outside the material.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In statements on centre of gravity versus centre of mass, the plumb line method, and toppling.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A uniform plate, forty centimetres by thirty, hangs at rest from a pin at one corner. What angle does its forty centimetre side make with the vertical? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. About thirty seven degrees.

A2.text: At rest, G is straight below the pin, at the centre of the plate.

A3.text: So the diagonal from the pin hangs straight down.

A4.text: The long side makes an angle theta with the diagonal. Tan theta is thirty over forty, so theta is about thirty seven degrees.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. Why must the plumb line from the pin pass through the centre of gravity?

Y3.text: Two. When are the centre of gravity and the centre of mass not the same point?

Y4.text: Three. Why does roof luggage make a bus tip over more easily?

N1.text: Next time: spin a ruler about its middle, then about its end. Why is one so much harder? Moment of inertia.
